strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across five benchmarks with proper methodology (5 seeds, multiple metrics, appropriate baselines)
Clear problem formulation as a POMDP with well-motivated reward decomposition combining RL and supervised learning
Consistent empirical improvements over HAM and random baselines, with APPLE-CrossQ demonstrating robustness across tasks without retuning
Strong commitment to reproducibility including detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, GPU specifications, and promised code release
Solid technical execution with correct POMDP formulation and proper algorithmic modifications to SAC/CrossQ
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of existing RL algorithms with minimal modifications (dynamic reward computation). The gradient decomposition in Eq. (3) is standard calculus without novel insights

Significantly overclaimed generality: evaluation limited exclusively to tactile sensing tasks in simulation, despite claims of 'diverse active perception problems.' No vision-based active perception evaluation despite extensive related work discussion

Problematic baseline comparison: HAM's CircleSquare failure appears partly due to LSTM architecture (APPLE-PPO-LSTM achieves only 72% vs. APPLE-PPO's 79%), not algorithmic limitations. MHSB task is severely limited (1,681 distinct values), making random baseline achieve 100% accuracy

Concerning sample efficiency requiring 5M training steps for relatively simple tasks (32×32 images, 2D actions), suggesting the transformer+RL combination may be inefficient. Paper acknowledges this but only proposes future work with pre-trained models
All experiments in simulation with no real-world validation, limiting practical applicability. GelSight simulator (Taxim) used exclusively; unclear how sim-to-real transfer would perform

Missing ablations on key design choices: shared transformer backbone benefit not quantified, discount factor sensitivity unanalyzed, action regularization coefficient impact untested. No principled explanation for SAC vs. CrossQ performance disparities across tasks

Insufficient policy analysis: limited visualization of learned exploration strategies (only 2 figures), minimal investigation into why APPLE-SAC dramatically underperforms on Toolbox (hyperparameter sensitivity despite robustness claims), no analysis of what makes APPLE-CrossQ more robust
No theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees. Assumption that predictions don't influence future states (Eq. 2) may be violated in complex scenarios. No principled guidance for method selection

Inconsistent performance across variants (APPLE-SAC vs. CrossQ) with dramatic differences on some tasks (Toolbox), suggesting hyperparameter sensitivity undermines claimed generality. Statistical significance tests not provided despite overlapping error bars

strengths: Well-motivated problem in active tactile perception with clear presentation of POMDP formulation and gradient decomposition
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple tasks (classification, regression, localization) with careful reproducibility practices and promised code release
Substantial empirical improvements over HAM baseline with lower sample complexity on several benchmarks
Detailed appendices with hyperparameter optimization, implementation details, and environment specifications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward engineering (adding -ℓ_π to reward function) rather than algorithmic innovation; gradient decomposition follows directly from basic calculus

Problematic baseline comparison: HAM was algorithmically modified (different reward function), CircleSquare task is acknowledged as trivial with only 1,681 distinct observations, and no comparison with modern off-policy RL methods or information-theoretic active learning approaches

Overstated generality claims: evaluation limited to tactile MNIST variants in simulation only; all tasks share similar structure (localized sensory input requiring spatial accumulation); no cross-domain transfer or handling of substantially different task structures demonstrated

Severe sample inefficiency contradicting practicality claims: requires 5-10M environment steps (40-50 GPU hours) for relatively simple tasks, undermining claims of being a 'general' framework; no mitigation beyond vague future work suggestions

Inconsistent behavior and hyperparameter sensitivity: APPLE-SAC fails on Toolbox while CrossQ succeeds without task-specific tuning; high variance on volume estimation; different hyperparameter sets needed for different configurations; claims of robustness based on limited evidence

Questionable methodological choices: RL reward merely regularizes action magnitude (10^-3 ||a_t||^2), suggesting direct gradient descent with L2 regularization would suffice; shared backbone justified only as 'empirically found' with no ablation or theory; Vision Transformer for 32×32 images appears over-engineered

Limited real-world applicability: all experiments in simulation with no robot validation; simple 2D action spaces with no evidence of scaling to high-dimensional spaces; single sensor evaluation without addressing multi-fingered scalability

Insufficient analysis: learned policies relegated to appendix without interpretation; no analysis of strategies learned vs. baselines; no investigation of design choice motivations beyond empirical observation; missing ablations on key components

strengths: Clear and principled POMDP formulation with elegant mathematical framework decomposing the objective into policy and prediction loss gradients
Versatile evaluation across five diverse benchmarks spanning classification, regression, and pose estimation tasks, demonstrating applicability beyond single-task methods
Strong empirical results with APPLE-CrossQ showing robust performance across tasks without hyperparameter retuning (e.g., 97% on CircleSquare vs HAM's random guessing)
Rigorous experimental methodology with 5 random seeds, extensive HEBO hyperparameter search, and thoughtful ablations isolating the benefits of off-policy learning
Demonstrates clear advantage of off-policy over on-policy RL through comprehensive comparisons (REINFORCE, PPO, SAC/CrossQ variants)
Strong reproducibility efforts with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, hardware specifications, and commitment to code release
Effective visualizations of learned exploration strategies (Figures 5, 14) demonstrating interpretability and strategic behavior
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: APPLE-SAC and APPLE-CrossQ are straightforward applications of existing RL algorithms with standard modifications (trajectory observations, prediction loss gradient); core contribution is primarily demonstrating off-policy RL works for active perception rather than proposing novel algorithms

Critical sample efficiency limitation: Requires 5-10M training steps for tactile tasks and 10M for Toolbox, prohibitively expensive for real robotics applications; inadequately addressed with only vague references to pre-trained models and no concrete experiments demonstrating improvements

No real robot validation: All experiments use simulated sensors (Taxim, simulated GelSight); the substantial sim-to-real gap for tactile sensing undermines claims of practical applicability and generality

Limited baseline comparisons: Only HAM and random baselines for main results; no comparison with other recent active perception methods (e.g., ActExplore); PPO variants relegated to appendix; missing comparisons with alternative off-policy methods

Overstated generality claims: Evaluation limited to tactile domain with only CircleSquare (28×28, 2 classes, color gradient) as a vision task; no evidence the approach generalizes to diverse modalities or complex vision problems

Task design concerns: MHSB task can be solved by memorization (~1,681 observation values), CircleSquare is overly simplified with directional guidance; Toolbox is more challenging but still relatively constrained; raises questions about true complexity of benchmarks

Architecture choices lack justification: No ablation on Vision Transformer choice vs CNNs; no comparison of shared backbone vs independent representations despite authors claiming empirical benefits; these choices significantly impact results
Hyperparameter sensitivity: APPLE-SAC fails on Toolbox without task-specific tuning; different hyperparameters needed for vision/non-vision configurations; undermines 'general framework' claim
Missing critical ablations: No ablation on discount factor γ, prediction loss weighting, episode length effects, or exploration-exploitation tradeoff analysis

Volume estimation weakness: TactileMNISTVolume shows notably worse performance with higher variance; authors acknowledge difficulty but provide insufficient analysis; suggests method may not be as robust to regression tasks

Fairness concerns in HAM comparison: HAM compared with modified reward function (negative prediction loss vs original binary reward); extensive tuning (10M steps) may not reflect realistic scenarios; difficult to isolate whether failures are algorithmic or implementation-specific

Notation and clarity issues: Tilde notation in Section 3.1 is somewhat confusing; weak connection to active learning literature (information gain, uncertainty sampling); could better explain why off-policy learning specifically addresses active perception challenges

strengths: Well-motivated POMDP formulation with elegant decomposition into policy and supervised learning gradients (Eq. 3)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with proper methodology: 5 random seeds, hyperparameter tuning, extensive ablations, detailed implementation details, and reproducibility statements
Strong empirical results across multiple active perception tasks (classification, regression, pose estimation) with substantial improvements over HAM baseline
Demonstrates cross-task generality without task-specific modifications; APPLE-CrossQ shows robustness across different domains
Clear presentation with well-structured paper, good figures, and thorough appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: decomposing objectives into policy and supervised gradients is conceptually straightforward; applying off-policy methods to this formulation is standard; distinction from internally rewarded RL (Li et al. 2023) appears incremental
Severe sample efficiency limitations (5M environment steps, 40-50 hours per run) acknowledged but not addressed; no attempted solutions undermines practical robotics applications
All experiments in simulation with relatively simple synthetic tasks (MNIST digits, binary classification, stationary objects); no real-world robot validation despite claiming relevance to robotics

Generality claims overstated: tasks involve stationary objects with fixed target properties; no evaluation on complex scenes, manipulation, shape reconstruction, or realistic visual complexity (CIFAR-10: 73% accuracy)

Incomplete baseline comparisons: only HAM compared; no comparison to other recent active perception methods, information-gain approaches, or Bayesian optimization; unfair comparison of off-policy (SAC/CrossQ) vs on-policy (REINFORCE) methods
Hyperparameter sensitivity despite generality claims: Table 1 shows APPLE-SAC requires different hyperparameters for vision vs non-vision tasks; extensive tuning needed

Insufficient analysis of learned behaviors: mostly qualitative; for TactileMNIST authors acknowledge strategies are 'less clear'; no systematic evaluation of exploration efficiency or information gain
Sparse reward handling tested only on one task (Section C.3) with degraded performance; insufficient for real-world applicability where ground-truth labels may be unavailable

Theoretical analysis absent: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or analysis of when the decomposition should work well; connection between prediction loss minimization and good exploration policies not rigorously established

Architectural choices under-justified: why Vision Transformer + Transformer over alternatives? Ablation shows LSTM worse but doesn't justify ViT; no ablation on shared vs separate embeddings across components

strengths: Clear POMDP formulation and elegant decomposition of objective into policy gradient and supervised loss components
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations, including sparse rewards, downstream tasks, and architectural comparisons
Well-presented paper with good motivation for active perception, particularly in tactile domain
Shared transformer architecture across policy/Q-networks/perception module is sensible design
Thorough implementation details, hyperparameter documentation, and reproducibility statements
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward combination of off-policy RL (SAC/CrossQ) + Transformers + supervised loss, with prior work on RL for active perception (HAM, RAM) well-established

Unfair comparison to HAM baseline: modified reward function (0-1 → prediction loss), asymmetric hyperparameter tuning effort, and HAM's eventual success with PPO (79% on CircleSquare vs APPLE's 97%) undermines claims of on-policy unsuitability

Generality claims severely overstated: evaluation limited to single benchmark suite (Tactile MNIST variants), only four tactile tasks plus CircleSquare/CIFAR10; doesn't demonstrate diversity across problem domains
Critical practical limitation: prohibitive sample complexity (5M steps, 40-50 hours) with no concrete solutions; acknowledged in paper but not addressed, making real-world deployment impractical

No real-world validation: all simulation experiments; tactile sensor sim-to-real transfer is notoriously difficult and untested for this approach; no analysis of scalability to multiple fingers/modalities

Problematic experimental design: inconsistent input representations (flat vectors vs. encoders) across tasks, high variance in results (TactileMNISTVolume), restricted baselines (only HAM + random), missing comparisons to recent active perception and off-policy methods
Task design issues: MHSB has only 1,681 unique observations (41×41 bins) making it trivially learnable via memorization; APPLE-RND reaches ~100%, suggesting task doesn't test policy learning
Unexplained failure modes: APPLE-SAC poor performance on Toolbox attributed to 'not tuned' without deeper analysis suggests instability or poor generalization

Technical concerns not addressed: dynamic loss recomputation in Bellman residual could cause bias/instability in off-policy learning; assumption that predictions don't affect states limits applicability

Missing critical analyses: no systematic sensitivity studies on discount factor, regularization, loss function design; limited quantitative analysis of learned exploration strategies despite qualitative claims

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation with elegant theoretical derivation showing gradient decomposition into policy gradient and supervised loss gradient
Principled framework enabling task-agnostic learning without hand-crafted heuristics, naturally accommodating classification, regression, and localization
Well-justified use of off-policy RL methods demonstrating substantial sample efficiency improvements over on-policy baselines (REINFORCE/PPO)
Comprehensive experimental work including multiple tasks, extensive ablation studies, detailed hyperparameter documentation, and reproducibility materials
Honest discussion of limitations (sample efficiency, simulation-only evaluation, narrow benchmark scope) rather than overselling results
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (transformers, SAC, CrossQ) with supervised learning; connection to internally rewarded RL (Li et al. 2023) suggests limited novelty

Generality claims significantly overstated: all non-toy experiments from single benchmark suite (Tactile MNIST); no visual active perception despite extensive literature; missing tasks (shape estimation, texture recognition) mentioned in introduction
Sample efficiency remains prohibitively high (5M steps ≈ 40-50 GPU hours), undermining practical applicability and contradicting efficiency claims; acknowledged but not adequately addressed

Unfair baseline comparison: HAM modified from original formulation (loss-based vs. binary reward), evaluated on tasks it wasn't designed for; MHSB benchmark trivial with only 1,681 discrete observations making random baseline nearly optimal
Complete absence of real robot experiments despite being robotics paper; simulation-only evaluation with acknowledged sim-to-real challenges for vision-based tactile sensors but no proposed solutions
Limited baseline comparisons: only HAM evaluated; missing information-theoretic baselines, other general active perception methods, and relevant visual active perception approaches
Hyperparameter sensitivity: APPLE-SAC fails on Toolbox without tuning; extensive HEBO optimization required; limited analysis of why APPLE-CrossQ is more robust
Statistical rigor gaps: only 5 random seeds, large variance in some results (TactileMNISTVolume), no significance testing; incomplete analysis of failure modes and design choices
